rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient that spans almost the full solvent range so all 10 compounds are likely to elute and reveal the overall retention window. A moderate 20 min slope balances information on selectivity with low risk of a truncated run.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is to reduce run time. Keep the same solvent window and temperature and shorten the gradient one step to test whether the critical cluster around peaks 5–7 remains above R = 1.5 while bringing the last peak closer to 10 min.

The 16 min method is nearly ideal and the limiting pair is still just above the 1.5 threshold, so the next best move is one more reduction in gradient time. This directly tests whether we can pull the last peak under 10 min without sacrificing full resolution of the 5–7 cluster.

At 14 min the only issue is the 6/7 pair, so keep the faster gradient and adjust selectivity with a small temperature decrease. Lowering T often increases retention and can improve separation of close pairs while likely keeping the last peak near or below 10 min.

Dropping temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing peaks 5/6, so probe in the opposite direction with a small temperature increase while keeping the fast 14 min gradient. This tests whether higher T can restore the critical cluster separation enough to exceed R = 1.5 while preserving t_last under 10 min.

Temperature changes both hurt the critical cluster, so keep 40 C and instead slightly narrow the gradient window at the strong end to make the effective gradient shallower where the late/mid peaks elute. That should preferentially spread peaks 5–7 while likely keeping the last peak near 10 min.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6/7 pair while still keeping t_last under 10 min, so continue one more step in the same direction. This should further shallow the effective gradient around the clustered peaks and may push the last sub-1.5 pair over the threshold with minimal time penalty.

At phi1 = 0.85 all pairs are now fully resolved, so the next optimization is to recover the small time penalty by shortening tG one step. This should test whether the improved selectivity from the narrower window is enough to keep the 6/7 pair at or above 1.5 while pulling t_last back under 10 min.

The 12 min gradient became too steep at phi1 = 0.85, so keep the shorter tG but slightly widen the window to phi1 = 0.90. This should restore some spacing for the critical 6/7 pair while maintaining a last peak comfortably under 10 min.

The best region is around tG 14 and phi1 0.85–0.90, with the 6/7 pair remaining critical; changing phi1 alone trades time against that pair. Raise phi0 one step to narrow the gradient range and reduce run time while probing whether the altered early gradient selectivity preserves full resolution in the mid-cluster.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the only remaining objective is to find the shortest method that still keeps every pair at R >= 1.5. Shorten tG one step from the current fully resolved optimum and test whether the 6/7 pair remains above threshold while pulling the last peak clearly below 10 min.

The current optimum is just at full resolution, while shortening to 12 min fails at the 6/7 pair. A small decrease in phi1 at the 14 min setting should further spread the critical mid/late cluster and may keep full resolution while moving us to the edge for later time reduction.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 gave the breakthrough 1.000 score by shortening retention without hurting the critical pair, so test one more step upward at the same successful phi1 and tG. This may pull t_last just under 10 min while retaining enough selectivity for peaks 6/7.

Injection 13 gives full resolution with t_last safely under 10 min, so now test whether the gradient can be shortened further while staying above the 1.5 threshold. This is the most direct way to search for a shorter equally optimal method around the new best region.

Increasing phi0 to 0.15 improved the fully resolved 14 min method and left a small resolution margin on the 6/7 pair, so one more step up may shorten retention further while still staying above R = 1.5. This explores whether the optimum can be pushed to an even faster fully resolved method at the same gradient time.

The best fully resolved methods sit at phi0 = 0.10–0.15, phi1 = 0.85, tG = 14, and raising phi0 further to 0.20 reduced the 6/7 margin too much. A small increase in phi1 from that strong-performing phi0 = 0.15 setting may rebalance selectivity around the critical pair while still keeping t_last under 10 min.

Both 0.10/0.85/14 and 0.15/0.85/14 achieve CRF 1.000, and the latter has slightly shorter retention but a bit less resolution margin. Lengthening the gradient while narrowing to phi1 = 0.80 tests whether we can keep full resolution with t_last still under 10 min, potentially identifying an even more robust optimum around the same score ceiling.

The strongest full-resolution region is centered on phi0 = 0.10–0.15 and phi1 = 0.85 with tG = 14; moving to 12 min consistently hurts the 6/7 pair. Testing the narrower window at phi1 = 0.80 together with the lower phi0 = 0.10 and shorter tG = 12 probes whether extra selectivity can recover that pair while keeping the run substantially faster.

The remaining unexplored corner near the best region is phi0 = 0.15 with the narrower phi1 = 0.80 at the shorter 12 min gradient. This checks whether the combined effect can preserve or improve the critical 6/7 resolution enough to create a shorter fully resolved method than the current 14 min optima.

We already have CRF 1.000 at 40 C, so with the remaining budget the key question is whether temperature can further shorten a fully resolved method without dropping the critical 6/7 pair below 1.5. Testing the proven 0.10/0.85/14 method at higher temperature directly probes that possibility.

Higher temperature strongly collapsed the critical 6/7 pair, so test the same proven method in the opposite direction. If 35 C maintains full resolution while keeping t_last near 10 min, it could reveal whether 40 C is truly optimal or whether cooler conditions offer a more robust fully resolved setting.

Temperature is clearly impactful on selectivity, but it has only been tested around the phi0 = 0.10 optimum; the phi0 = 0.15 optimum may respond differently. With few injections left and CRF already maxed, this run probes whether the faster-retaining 0.15/0.85/14 method can stay fully resolved at higher temperature and potentially define a more aggressive equally optimal option.

Both hotter and cooler temperatures disrupted the critical cluster for the phi0 = 0.10 optimum, but the phi0 = 0.15 optimum has not yet been checked at lower temperature. This final temperature probe will confirm whether 40 C is uniquely best in that region or whether a cooler variant can also retain full resolution with acceptable time.

40 C is clearly optimal, and the main remaining uncertainty is whether a stronger starting composition combined with a narrower window can still maintain the critical 6/7 separation while shortening retention. This unexplored combination is close to the best region and could reveal a faster edge-of-failure condition to bracket the true optimum more tightly.

The new 0.20/0.80/14 method matches the best CRF with full resolution and t_last well under 10 min, making it the strongest candidate for one final shortening test. Reducing tG to 12 min is the highest-value last injection because it could uncover a shorter still-fully-resolved optimum; if it fails, the 14 min method remains confirmed.
